title: terminate called without an active exception terminate called recursively terminate called recursively
body:
Our service has been running fine, however, it has recently started to experience the following problem:

![image](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/assets/79587688/35e21de8-6cc3-4842-846b-38ec0bbd35f3)

It will appear every time we restart

![image](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/assets/79587688/ee066192-9cf1-45c0-8d64-f55293fe26c2)

From docker, he is running fine, but cannot be accessed through any port

![image](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/assets/79587688/a927a6b3-5075-4024-b137-2a8c03653978)

comments.author: reporter

comments.body:
I doubled the memory, but it still doesn't work. Let me summarize:

Problem performance:
1. Log prompt: terminate called without an active exception
terminate called recursively
2. Reading and writing operations cannot be performed normally.
3. Port access 6333 6334 6335 prompts: Connection refused
4. The dashboard cannot be accessed normally. This should be because when accessing port 6333, a Connection refused message is displayed.

I did the following:
1. Restart the service.
2. Double the memory upgrade.

I now need to understand the cause of this problem and how to get my service back to normal.

Using three machines for sharding, the data volume of a single machine is approximately 429 G.

## compose
```yaml
version: '3.5'

services:
  qdrant:
    container_name: qdrant
    image: qdrant/qdrant:v1.6.0
    environment:
      - QDRANT__CLUSTER__ENABLED=true
    tty: true
    ports:
      - "6333:6333"
      - "6334:6334"
      - "6335:6335"
    volumes:
      - /disk/ssd1/qdrant-node/storage:/disk/storage
      - /disk/ssd1/qdrant-node/snapshots:/disk/snapshots
      - /disk/ssd1/qdrant-node/config/production.yaml:/qdrant/config/production.yaml
    command: /qdrant/qdrant --uri http://qdrantHost:6335
    networks:
     - qrant

networks:
  qrant:
    driver: bridge
    ipam:
      driver: default
      config:
      - subnet: 21.88.12.0/24
        gateway: 21.88.12.1
```

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: @participant2 I think I can reproduce the problem, which refers to the terminate called recursively error. I rebuilt a three-machine sharded cluster with version 1.9.1. I re-imported the previous data into the three-slice cluster and I used the following method. 1. Write to three machines on average. 2. Each batch of 1,000 pieces of data is written, and approximately 5,000 - 10,000 pieces of data are written every second, that is, 5 - 10 batches of data are written in parallel. Then after a night like this, shard dead and shard partial appeared. When I restarted the service, a terminate called recursively error occurred. I think the reason for this problem is that the processing speed of qdrant cannot keep up with the writing speed, that is, the writing traffic is too large, causing the internal sharding to collapse. This has nothing to do with whether there are multiple collections, it is purely due to the excessive amount of writing. Is there any good fix for qdrant in this regard?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I think an excellent vector database can support high concurrent writes.

If the amount of writing is too large, you can directly reject the latest written data and return an exception error. In this case, the problem will be easier to troubleshoot.

And we may only need to add a retry mechanism, or use a message queue to cut peaks and fill valleys.

By the way, our data volume is relatively large, for example, when I imported from the backup database this time, I wrote about 20 million vector data an hour.

It took us more than ten hours of writing to recover less than half the data.

In addition, each vector data is 512 dimensions, with three payload parameters.

So, I suspect it's a problem with large volumes of writing.

In addition, our disk is using ssd, we have tried to use mechanical hard disk before, and found that it was completely unable to meet expectations.
